name: AP Research
overview: AP Research is the second course in the AP Capstone program. Each student designs and carries out a year-long investigation of a question of their choosing, using an appropriate research method, and reports it in an academic paper and a presentation with an oral defense. The course builds on AP Seminar's QUEST framework, with a focus on research methods, ethics, and contributing new understanding to a scholarly conversation.
examMode: No sit-down exam; the paper is submitted through the AP Digital Portfolio and the presentation is scored by the teacher

sections.name: Academic paper
sections.notes: 4,000–5,000 words, scored by College Board. Typically includes an introduction and literature review, method, results or findings, discussion and analysis, conclusion and future directions, and a bibliography.

sections.name: Presentation and oral defense
sections.notes: A 15–20 minute multimedia presentation followed by three or four questions from a panel of three evaluators, scored by the teacher.

skills.name: Question and Explore
skills.description: Find a gap in the scholarly conversation and write a focused, feasible research question.

skills.name: Understand and Analyze
skills.description: Read scholarly studies critically, including their methods and data.

skills.name: Evaluate Multiple Perspectives
skills.description: Situate your work in the literature, weigh conflicting findings, and conduct research ethically.

skills.name: Synthesize Ideas
skills.description: Choose and justify a method, collect and analyze data, and draw conclusions that create new understanding.

skills.name: Team, Transform, and Transmit
skills.description: Communicate your research in academic writing and an oral defense, and reflect on your process.

scoring.summary: The academic paper is 75% of the AP score and the presentation and oral defense 25%. There is no multiple-choice or timed free-response section. Both parts are scored with analytic rubrics published on AP Central; Klutch's practice tasks use simplified point scales, not the official rubric rows.

frqTypes.name: Research skill task
frqTypes.howScored: Klutch practice scale shown with each task, covering accuracy, justification, and specificity for tasks such as writing a research question, critiquing a method, or answering an oral defense question.

strategy: Choose a narrow question where you can collect your own data; a feasible small study beats an ambitious impossible one.
Build the literature review around themes and debates, ending with the gap your study fills.
Justify your method by explaining why it fits your question better than the alternatives.
Get approval from your school's review process before collecting data from people.
Report results before interpreting them, then discuss limitations honestly and say what your findings add.
Rehearse the oral defense with likely questions: why this method, what surprised you, what you would change.
pitfalls: A question too broad, or one that only summarizes existing research instead of creating new understanding.
Claiming causation from correlational or survey data.
Overgeneralizing from a small or convenience sample.
A literature review that summarizes sources one by one instead of synthesizing them.
Hiding limitations instead of discussing them.
caveats: Klutch's practice tasks use simplified point scales, not College Board's rubric rows; use the official rubrics on AP Central when drafting your paper.
All study abstracts and scenarios in Klutch's practice are fictional.
